lessons.title: Read and write sets
lessons.summary: List the elements of a set, count distinct members and use Cambridge's Extended membership and subset symbols.
lessons.objective: List the elements of a set, count distinct members and use Cambridge's Extended membership and subset symbols.
lessons.before: Know what the answer represents before you start.
lessons.ideas:
In \(\{x:x\text{ is an integer},\;-3

\(n(A)\) asks how many distinct elements are in \(A\). It gives a number. A list of the elements gives a set.

\(3\in B\) says that the number 3 belongs to \(B\). \(\{3\}\subseteq B\) says that all members of the set \(\{3\}\) are in \(B\). Their negative forms are \(\notin\) and \(\nsubseteq\).
lessons.method:
How do I turn a rule into a list?

Read one boundary at a time. A strict sign excludes its endpoint. Write the candidates in order so you can check that every allowed integer is present.

How do I count the members?

Cross out repeated copies. Count each remaining entry once and give the count as a number.

Extended: Is it a member or a subset?

One missing element is enough to rule out a subset. The empty set \(\varnothing\) has no members and is a subset of every set. Equal sets are subsets of each other.
mistakes: A list of integers stops at the next integer. If the rule allows all real numbers, the interval contains more than the integers you can list.
A set with one member is not the same answer as a count of one. In a question asking for the set, keep the braces even around one entry.
\(\varnothing\) and \(\{0\}\) mean different things. The first set has no elements. The second has one element, the number zero.

examples.title: List the integers in a set
examples.question: Write all the elements of \(A=\{x:x\text{ is an integer},\;2<x\leq 9\}\).
examples.solution:
Read the condition from left to right. Begin at the first integer greater than \(2\), which is \(3\).

The sign \(\leq\) includes the upper endpoint \(9\). The set is \(\{3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9\}\).

examples.title: Count distinct elements
examples.question: \(D=\{31,23,26,29,31\}\). Find \(n(D)\).
examples.solution:
The repeated entry \(31\) is the same element each time. Write the distinct elements as \(\{23, 26, 29, 31\}\).

Count the members of that set. \(n(D)=4\).

examples.title: Choose the membership symbol
examples.question:
Let \(A=\{28,31\}\). Complete \(34\;\square\;A\) with the correct symbol.

A. \(\in\)   B. \(\notin\)   C. \(\subseteq\)   D. \(\nsubseteq\)
examples.solution:
The object on the left is the number \(34\), so we need a membership symbol.

The number is absent from the list. Use \(\notin\).

lessons.title: Two-set Venn diagrams
lessons.summary: Place each element in a two-set Venn diagram and read union, intersection, complement and bracketed expressions.
lessons.objective: Place each element in a two-set Venn diagram and read union, intersection, complement and bracketed expressions.
lessons.before: Read a region, then check what the set operation asks for.
lessons.ideas:
The rectangle represents \(\mathcal{E}\), the universal set. The shared lens represents \(A\cap B\). The corner outside both circles is still part of \(\mathcal{E}\).

\(A\cup B\) includes A only, both and B only. \(A\cap B\) includes the overlap only.

\(A'\) contains everything in \(\mathcal{E}\) outside \(A\). That includes the B-only part and the space outside both circles.

\((A\cup B)'=A'\cap B'\) is outside both circles. \((A\cap B)'=A'\cup B'\) is everything except the lens.
lessons.method:
Where does each element go?

Place shared entries in the lens first. Then fill the A-only and B-only parts. Every remaining entry in the universe belongs outside both circles. If the sets have no shared entries, they are called disjoint.

Which regions belong to ‘A or B’?

Take every entry in at least one circle. Make a single list and check that a shared entry appears only once.

How do I find the complement?

Trace the boundary of A. Keep every entry within the rectangle but outside that boundary. Reject entries in the lens because they are inside A.

Extended: What do the brackets change?

Sketch the region named in brackets, then keep the rest of the rectangle. To represent ‘A only’ directly use \(A\cap B'\).
mistakes: A shared number appears once in the lens. Writing it separately in A and B creates two copies of one element.
If the question says ‘exactly one’, leave the lens out. If it says ‘at least one’, include the lens.
A complement is tied to its rectangle. Do not write numbers or objects that were never in the universal set.
Look at what the prime touches. A prime after a closing bracket acts on everything in the brackets.

examples.title: Find the entries in the overlap
examples.question:
The universal set \(\mathcal{E}\) contains the integers from \(38\) to \(45\), inclusive.

\(A\) = \(\{38, 40, 42, 44\}\) and \(B\) = \(\{38, 41, 43, 44\}\).

List the elements of \(A\cap B\).
examples.solution:
Compare each entry in \(A\) with the list for \(B\).

Only \(\{38, 44\}\) appears in both lists. Write these elements once in the overlap.

examples.title: List the union
examples.question:
The universal set \(\mathcal{E}\) contains the integers from \(42\) to \(49\), inclusive.

\(A\) = \(\{43, 45, 47, 49\}\) and \(B\) = \(\{44, 47, 48, 49\}\).

List the elements of \(A\cup B\).
examples.solution:
Take the elements in \(A\) then add any elements of \(B\) that do not appear in that list.

Include the shared elements once. \(A\cup B\) is \(\{43, 44, 45, 47, 48, 49\}\).

examples.title: Find a complement
examples.question:
The universal set \(\mathcal{E}\) contains the integers from \(46\) to \(53\), inclusive.

\(A\) = \(\{46, 48, 50, 51\}\) and \(B\) = \(\{47, 48, 51, 52\}\).

List the elements of \(A′\).
examples.solution:
Start with every element in \(\mathcal{E}\). Cross out those inside \(A\), including its overlap with \(B\).

The remaining B-only and outside entries form \(\{47, 49, 52, 53\}\).

examples.title: Find the complement of the union
examples.question:
The universal set \(\mathcal{E}\) contains the integers from \(50\) to \(57\), inclusive.

\(A\) = \(\{50, 52, 54, 56\}\) and \(B\) = \(\{50, 53, 55, 56\}\).

List the elements of \((A\cup B)\prime\).
examples.solution:
Work inside the brackets first. \(A\cup B\) contains \(\{50, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56\}\).

Remove all of these from the rectangle. The elements outside both circles are \(\{51, 57\}\).

lessons.title: Solve problems with two-set totals
lessons.summary: Read counts from four regions, reconstruct an overlap or a missing outside count, and check that the numbers fit.
lessons.objective: Read counts from four regions, reconstruct an overlap or a missing outside count, and check that the numbers fit.
lessons.before: Keep whole-circle totals and separate region counts apart.
lessons.ideas:
With counts, add the numbers in the requested regions. Each person, response or object belongs to one region.

\(n(A\cup B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cap B)\). The subtraction removes the extra copy of the overlap.

\(n(A\cap B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cup B)\). When neither is given, first find \(n(A\cup B)\) by subtracting neither from \(n(\mathcal{E})\).
lessons.method:
Do the numbers name entries or count them?

For \(n(A\cup B)\), add A only, the overlap and B only. For \(n(A)\), add A only and the overlap. For the total, also add neither.

Why do whole-circle totals double-count?

Fill in the overlap first. From each circle total subtract the overlap to get its exclusive part. Then find the outside by subtracting the union from the overall total.

How can I recover a missing overlap?

Fill all four regions and recombine them to verify both original circle totals. All four entries must be whole numbers and at least zero.
mistakes: A number printed in a region might be a label, such as code 12. A label counts as one element. A region count of 12 already represents twelve elements.
The given value of n(A) belongs to all of the A circle. Putting it into A only and then adding the lens changes the stated circle total.
A negative number of people signals that the information or your interpretation is inconsistent. Check whether a value describes ‘only’ or a whole circle.

examples.title: Find the size of a union
examples.question:
A record of workshop bookings groups the entries into \(A\) for ceramics and \(B\) for woodwork.

RegionEntries
A only8
Both5
B only6
Neither9

Find \(n(A\cup B)\).
examples.solution:
Include A only, both and B only. Leave the 9 entries outside the circles.

Add the three separate regions. \(8+5+6=19\).

examples.title: Recover the outside count
examples.question:
A record of workshop bookings groups the entries into \(A\) for ceramics and \(B\) for woodwork.

There are 34 entries altogether. \(n(A)=16\), \(n(B)=13\) and 4 entries belong to both sets.

How many entries belong to neither set?
examples.solution:
Adding the whole circles gives \(16+13=29\). This counts the 4 shared entries twice.

Subtract the overlap once. The union contains \(29-4=25\) entries.

Subtract the union from the total to find neither. \(34-25=9\).

examples.title: Work backwards to find both
examples.question:
A record of workshop bookings groups the entries into \(A\) for ceramics and \(B\) for woodwork.

There are 32 entries. 11 are in \(A\), 15 are in \(B\) and 9 are in neither.

How many entries belong to both sets?
examples.solution:
The union has \(32-9=23\) entries. It counts everyone in at least one group once.

The two circle totals add to \(26\). The extra count is the overlap: \(26-23=3\).

lessons.title: Three-set Venn diagrams (Extended)
lessons.summary: Use all eight regions of a three-set diagram, reconstruct pair-only counts and combine operations in the correct order.
lessons.objective: Use all eight regions of a three-set diagram, reconstruct pair-only counts and combine operations in the correct order.
lessons.before: Fill the three-set diagram from the centre outwards.
lessons.ideas:
Exactly two gives the three pair-only regions. At least two also includes the centre. None of the sets contains the outside region.

\(n(A\cap C\cap B')=n(A\cap C)-n(A\cap B\cap C)\). The same method works for the other pairs.

For \((A\cup B)\cap C\), first allow A or B. Keep only regions inside C. The centre passes both tests.
lessons.method:
Where are the eight regions?

Name a region before entering a value. Use one circle label for an exclusive single region, two labels for a pair-only region, and all three for the centre.

Why start with the triple intersection?

Complete the three pair-only regions next. In each whole circle, subtract its two pair-only regions and the centre to get only that circle. Fill the outside last.

How do I read a longer expression?

Mark the eligible regions with a finger or a little tick. Compare each region with the whole expression before adding counts. If a whole bracket has a prime, keep precisely the other regions.
mistakes: The outside is a valid region inside the rectangle. Include it when checking the total or finding the entries in none.
‘A and C’ allows B as well. ‘A and C only’ places those entries outside B.
C only passes the C test. It fails the A-or-B test, so leave it out of the expression above.

examples.title: Count entries in exactly two sets
examples.question:
A technician lists testing stations. Sets \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) record entries for light, noise and temperature, in that order.

RegionEntries
A only4
B only8
C only4
A and B only8
A and C only2
B and C only7
All three6
None11

How many entries are in exactly two sets?
examples.solution:
Use the three regions labelled ‘and … only’. Exclude the central region because those entries are in three sets.

Add those regions: \(8+2+7=17\).

examples.title: Recover a pair-only region
examples.question:
A community centre lists sessions. Sets \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) record entries for bouldering, printmaking and coding, in that order.

\(n(A\cap C)=10\). There are 4 entries in all three sets.

Find the number of entries in both \(A\) and \(C\), but outside \(B\).
examples.solution:
The 10 entries in \(A\cap C\) include those in \(B\) as well.

Remove the centre once. The pair-only count is \(10-4=6\).

examples.title: Apply a bracketed set operation
examples.question:
A nursery records garden plots. Sets \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) record entries for sage, mint and thyme, in that order.

RegionEntries
A only7
B only8
C only2
A and B only3
A and C only2
B and C only3
All three2
None10

Find \(n((A\cup B)\cap C)\).
examples.solution:
First identify all regions in \(A\cup B\). Then keep only the ones inside \(C\).

Use A-and-C only, B-and-C only and all three. \(2+3+2=7\).
